finding.description: Describes a defect in the same-role review, not a candidate defect already captured by a supported review finding.

reviewFindingAdjudication.description: Judges one finding made by the same-role review rather than judging the candidate defect again.

findingIds.description: Links only adjudicator findings that explain why this review finding is rejected; this array is empty when judgment is supported.

surfaceAdjudication.description: Echoes the bound same-role review assessment in reviewAssessmentJudgment and judges the soundness of that assessment in judgment. A sound blocking review assessment is blocking plus supported, not an adjudication failure.

findingIds.description: Links only adjudicator findings that explain a rejected same-role review assessment. It is empty for supported; rejected requires a linked blocking finding on this surface.

judgment.description: supported approves the same-role review assessment even when reviewAssessmentJudgment is blocking; rejected means the assessment is unsound or incomplete.

reviewAssessmentJudgment.description: Exact echo of the bound same-role review assessment's judgment; the deterministic verifier rejects any mismatch.

adjudicationSchema.description: This record judges the soundness and completeness of the same-role review, not the candidate.

findings.description: Adjudicator findings describe defects in the same-role review's requirement, assessment, reasoning, finding, coverage, or severity; they do not repeat candidate defects already captured by supported review findings.

reviewFindingAdjudications.description: Each entry judges one same-role review finding. A supported review finding has no adjudicator-finding links; a rejected review finding requires a linked blocking adjudicator finding that explains the review defect.

surfaceAdjudications.description: Each entry exactly echoes the same-role review assessment's pass, advisory, or blocking judgment, then separately judges that assessment as supported or rejected; it does not judge the candidate surface directly.

verdict.description: pass means the same-role review is sound and complete, even when that review correctly fails the candidate; fail means the same-role review is unsound or incomplete. This verdict never judges the candidate directly.

adjudicationSchema.title: Independent canonical-English semantic adjudication record

adjudicationSemantics.failMeaning: The same-role review is unsound or incomplete.
adjudicationSemantics.findingLinkMeaning: A supported surface assessment or review finding has no adjudicator-finding links; a rejected one links at least one blocking adjudicator finding on an overlapping surface that explains a defect in the review.
adjudicationSemantics.passMeaning: The same-role review is sound and complete, even when that review correctly fails the candidate.
adjudicationSemantics.subject: same-role-review
adjudicationSemantics.surfaceAdjudicationMeaning: Each surface adjudication exactly echoes the bound review assessment judgment in reviewAssessmentJudgment, then uses judgment supported or rejected to judge that assessment.

Reproduce the target variance, standard deviation, and uniform bound for fan-in 2 and fan-out 2.
Recalculate the target variance, standard deviation, and uniform bound for fan-in 4 and fan-out 2, and explain the reduced starting scale.
Inspect the zero-weight SiLU graph and derive the two input-weight gradient columns from the equal output weights and input signs.
Reproduce the same seed, shape, fan values, and construction order; compare the stored tensor values rather than only printed decimals.
Inspect the selected seed-18 tensor comparison with seed 17 for shape [2,2], fan-in 2, and fan-out 2; explain why the observed stored-weight difference does not establish uniqueness for every possible seed.
Explain why one finite [2,2] tensor need not have measured variance exactly 1/2.
Inspect the query-projection/token-table collection; identify its declaration order and distinguish a clone from an equal reconstruction.
Inspect the invalid-name, zero-fan, and duplicate calls; explain why caller state is unchanged and identify the duplicate indices.
Check the Transformer paper’s initializer boundary and distinguish it from attention-score or embedding forward scaling.
Explain how the near-linear and independence assumptions limit the variance argument, distinguishing a target weight-distribution variance from a guarantee that every decoder signal retains its variance.
For fan-in 2 and fan-out 2, target variance is 0.5, standard deviation is 0.707106781187, and uniform bound is 1.224744871392. Standard deviation measures distribution spread; the bound marks its endpoint.
For fan-in 4 and fan-out 2, target variance is 1/3, standard deviation is 0.577350269190, and uniform bound is 1.000000000000. Increasing the number of summed inputs reduces the requested weight spread under the compromise.
In the zero-weight SiLU graph, input x=[1,-1], equal output weights [1,1], and scalar backward seed one give both input-weight gradient columns [0.5,-0.5]^\top. SiLU is evaluated at zero, where its derivative is 1/2. The equal output weights give both units the same upstream factor; multiplying by the two input coordinates supplies the opposite signs.
The same implementation, starting generator state, shape, fan values, and construction order reproduce all tensor bits. The twelve-decimal display rounds those values and is not the strongest equality check.
With shape [2,2], fan-in 2, fan-out 2, and construction order unchanged, the selected seed-18 tensor values differ from those from seed 17. This one comparison does not prove that all possible seed/request pairs produce unique tensors.
The target weight variance is a property of the sampling distribution. A finite matrix can have a nonzero measured mean and a different measured variance without violating the rule.
decoder.block.0.attention.query.weight appears first, then token_embedding.weight. A clone shares the original tape leaf; an independently reconstructed equal tensor has another leaf.
The invalid name is rejected before widths or draws; zero fan-in is rejected before sampling. The caller receives trial state only on success. In the two-clone collection, the first occurrence is index 0 and the repeated occurrence index 1.
Vaswani et al. do not prescribe a parameter initializer. Attention-score and embedding scaling are operations in the forward model, not initial-value selection.
The forward/backward scale argument assumes independent zero-centered weights, independent zero-centered input features, and zero-centered arriving gradients, each group with its own common variance. Weights must be independent of the inputs and arriving gradients, and the activation is assumed symmetric and near-linear with unit slope. The target belongs to the sampling distribution; finite samples need not match it exactly. Nonlinearities, normalization, residual paths, depth, data, and optimization affect actual decoder signals, so no exact decoder-signal variance is guaranteed.

\operatorname{fan}_{in} | The count of input coordinates whose weighted contributions are summed into each output.
\operatorname{fan}_{out} | The count of output coordinates to which each input contributes.

Chapter 17 terms for starting weight spread, equal-unit symmetry, and exact replay.
Fan-in The count of input coordinates whose weighted contributions are summed into each output.
Fan-out The count of output coordinates to which each input contributes.
Hidden-unit symmetry Identical hidden units receive equal gradients under equal downstream treatment; equal updates keep them identical.
Parameter initialization Assigning the trainable values from which later optimization starts.
Pseudorandom generator A state-driven deterministic algorithm that supplies random-like draws, not cryptographic security.
Reproducibility Recreating identical stored weights with the same implementation, generator state, request, and construction order.
Seed The generator's raw starting state before its first draw; the same state gives the same continuation.
Target variance The chosen spread of a weight distribution in squared weight units, not a finite matrix's measured spread.
Uniform bound The endpoint magnitude of the zero-centered uniform interval used to sample weights.
Xavier-style initialization Zero-centered sampling that balances forward and backward width effects under independence and near-linear assumptions.

<h2 id="a-correct-gradient-still-needs-a-useful-starting-point">A correct gradient still needs a useful starting point</h2>
<p>Chapter 16 can differentiate a matrix transformation, but the backward pass
cannot choose its initial weights. In a bias-free layer, two hidden units
receiving the same input through the same activation compute the same feature
when their incoming weight columns match. If the downstream calculation treats
them equally, both receive the same gradient column. Applying equal updates
then keeps the units identical: training has not given them separate features.</p>
<p>Weight scale is a second problem. Each matrix output adds contributions from
several inputs, so changing the number of contributions can change the spread
of the resulting signal. Repeating matrix transformations can compound that
scale change. We need starting weights that distinguish the selected hidden
units, account for matrix width, and can be reproduced while comparing changes
to the model.</p>
<h3 id="work-through-one-sampled-projection">Work through one sampled projection</h3>
<p>Use a projection of shape <code>[2,2]</code>: its two rows correspond to input coordinates
and its two columns to output coordinates. Start the generator at seed <code>17</code>.

the identical-column condition described above. That fact is a starting-point
comparison, not evidence that the model has already learned useful features.</p>
<p>Restarting the same construction from seed <code>17</code> reproduces the stored tensor
bit for bit. The same selected request from seed <code>18</code> produces a different
tensor. Exact replay needs the same generator state, shape, fan values, and
construction order, not just a remembered seed after other parameters have
already consumed draws. The seed-<code>18</code> result is one observed comparison, not a
promise that every pair of seeds yields different tensors.</p>

<h2 id="let-both-matrix-widths-determine-the-starting-spread">Let both matrix widths determine the starting spread</h2>
<p>For the stored matrix <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.1389em">W</span></span></span></span>, weight <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.9694em;vertical-align:-0.2861em"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.1389em">W</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3117em"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.1389em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight" style="margin-right:0.0572em">ij</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2861em"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> connects input coordinate <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6595em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">i</span></span></span></span> to
output coordinate <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.854em;vertical-align:-0.1944em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0572em">j</span></span></span></span>. Fan-in counts the weighted inputs summed into each
output; fan-out counts the outputs receiving each input.</p>
<p>We estimate scale in a simplified setting: independent zero-centered dense
weights with a common variance, independent zero-centered input features with
a common variance,
weight/input independence, and a symmetric activation near a unit-slope linear
regime. The analogous backward estimate uses zero-centered arriving gradients
with a common variance, independent of the weights.</p>
<p>Under these assumptions, the forward signal’s variance is multiplied by fan-in
and weight variance. The backward gradient’s variance instead involves fan-out
and weight variance. Keeping either multiplier at one asks for the reciprocal
of its width; unequal widths ask for different scales.</p>

The standard deviation is the square root of the target variance. Standard
deviation and bound are both in weight units, but the bound marks the interval
endpoint rather than the typical spread around the mean.</p>
<p>SiLU does not exactly meet the
activation assumption. Normalization, residual paths, data, and optimization
also matter in the eventual decoder; the formula is not a decoder-wide
variance-preservation theorem.</p>
<h3 id="turn-the-distribution-into-repeatable-rust-samples">Turn the distribution into repeatable Rust samples</h3>
<p>A bound alone does not choose individual weights. <code>SplitMix64</code> supplies the
repeatable draws. Its seed is the raw <code>u64</code> state before the first increment,
so seed zero is valid. Wrapping integer operations advance and mix that state.
Dividing the integer in the high 53 mixed bits by the number of possible
53-bit values gives a binary64 fraction in <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1)</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">0</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span>. A fixed state gives the same
continuation. This is deterministic pseudorandom sampling, not
cryptographic randomness or ideal continuous sampling.</p>

<p><code>xavier_scale</code> first rejects zero widths and an overflowing integer fan sum.
It then stores the formula’s variance in <code>target_variance</code>, its square root in
<code>standard_deviation</code>, and the sampling bound in <code>uniform_limit</code>. The sampler
doubles a unit draw, subtracts one to center it, and multiplies by
<code>uniform_limit</code>. One draw supplies each weight in row-major order, so the
matrix shape fixes how many draws construction consumes.</p>

<p>The scale calculations and weights use <code>f64</code>. Integer checks happen before
conversion, but a sufficiently large valid <code>usize</code> count can round when cast
to <code>f64</code>. Division, square roots, and multiplication also use represented
arithmetic. The generator’s finite grid and the stored values therefore differ
from an ideal continuous distribution; printing twelve decimals rounds the
stored value again. Bit-for-bit replay is an implementation result, not a claim
that a finite matrix’s variance must equal the mathematical target. These small
examples do not exercise floating-point underflow or overflow; the checked
overflow errors concern integer dimensions.</p>

<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span>: the target variance becomes <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/3</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">1/3</span></span></span></span>, standard deviation <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.577350269190</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.577350269190</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">0.577350269190</span></span></span></span>,
and bound <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.000000000000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.000000000000</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1.000000000000</span></span></span></span>. More input contributions require a smaller starting
spread under the compromise. Width must therefore be known before sampling.</p>
<h3 id="keep-parameter-construction-replayable">Keep parameter construction replayable</h3>
<p>A sampled matrix must become a trainable <code>TensorValue</code> leaf so later backward
passes can accumulate its gradients. <code>NamedParameter</code> also gives that leaf a
stable external name, such as <code>decoder.block.0.attention.query.weight</code>.
The name identifies the parameter’s role across reconstruction; it is not the
runtime node itself. Cloning a parameter shares its tape leaf, while constructing
a new leaf with equal values does not.</p>
<p>Names need a fixed grammar and collections need duplicate rejection so name
lookup cannot silently select an ambiguous parameter. Declaration order stays
deliberate: on one shared generator stream, each successful construction
consumes the draws that precede the next parameter. Inserting an earlier matrix
changes the later samples.</p>
<p>A rejected request must not shift that stream. Name and width checks reject
invalid requests before drawing, and checked dimension arithmetic prevents a
wrapped storage count. Sampling uses a cloned trial generator; the caller’s
state is committed only after tensor and trainable-leaf construction succeed.
Every returned sampler error therefore leaves the caller’s state unchanged.
Correcting a failed request can reuse its intended starting state.</p>

<p>The parameter kinds need not share one starting value. Our later decoder uses
Xavier-style uniform matrix weights, optional zero biases, and RMSNorm gains
of one. Zero biases add no initial offset, and unit gains apply no additional
feature scaling after normalization. The token table reuses the sampler with
vocabulary size and feature width as its shape inputs; that convention does not
follow from a variance calculation for selecting a row.</p>

<h2 id="from-random-word-features-to-width-aware-repeated-projections">From random word features to width-aware repeated projections</h2>
<p>The earlier language-model example is
<a href="https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf">Bengio et al., <em>A Neural Probabilistic Language Model</em></a>.
Bengio et al. jointly train a word-feature matrix and neural matrices for next-word prediction. They report initializing the word features randomly, as for neural-network weights.</p>
<p>Random word features gave early neural language models trainable starting values, but randomness alone does not choose a scale for each matrix width. Bengio et al. do not specify a dimension-aware reproducible initialization rule; repeated transformations make that missing scale choice more consequential.</p>
<p>Glorot and Bengio connect starting weight variance to both forward and backward matrix widths under near-linear and independence assumptions. Transformers later combine learned embeddings with repeated attention and feed-forward projections, so many separately shaped trainable matrices need starting values.</p>
<p>The variance-aware analysis is
<a href="https://proceedings.mlr.press/v9/glorot10a/glorot10a.pdf">Glorot and Bengio, <em>Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks</em></a>.
Glorot and Bengio derive a compromise between fan-in and fan-out variance conditions under simplifying assumptions: target weight variance is 2 divided by the sum of the widths, implemented with a normalized zero-centered uniform distribution.</p>
<p>The later architecture is
<a href="https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2017/file/3f5ee243547dee91fbd053c1c4a845aa-Paper.pdf">Vaswani et al., <em>Attention Is All You Need</em></a>.
Vaswani et al. use learned embeddings and repeat query, key, value, attention-output, and two feed-forward projections in Transformer layers. Their paper does not prescribe a parameter initializer.</p>
<p>Our decoder uses reproducible Xavier-style uniform matrix samples, stable parameter names, zero optional biases, and RMSNorm gains of one. Its token table reuses the sampler by matrix shape. These are explicit construction policies: the Transformer paper does not prescribe them, and they do not guarantee exact variance preservation through SiLU, normalization, or residual paths.</p>
<p>The Transformer’s attention-score and embedding scaling act during forward
computation; they are not instructions for choosing initial weights. Likewise,
the papers do not define our raw-seed mapping, name grammar, construction order,
or error policy. The Rust contrast below isolates an initialization failure
condition without claiming to reproduce the historical models.</p>

<h2 id="inspect-equal-gradients-and-construction-guarantees">Inspect equal gradients and construction guarantees</h2>
<p>The sampled projection avoids identical columns in the selected request.
The zero-weight contrast shows why that distinction matters. Set
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=[1,-1]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.4306em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">x</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span><span class="mrel">=</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em"></span></span><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">−</span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span>, use a zero <code>[2,2]</code> input matrix, apply SiLU, and combine the two
hidden values with equal output weights <code>[1,1]</code>. Both hidden values and the
scalar output are zero.</p>
<p>The reverse pass is seeded with one at that scalar output. Equal output weights
give both hidden units the same upstream factor. SiLU’s derivative at zero is
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord">1/2</span></span></span></span>, and each input weight multiplies that factor by its input coordinate.
Both gradient columns are therefore <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>0.5</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">⊤</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.5,-0.5]^\top</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1.0991em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">0.5</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">−</span><span class="mord">0.5</span><span class="mclose"><span class="mclose">]</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8491em"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em"></span><span class="sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight">⊤</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, stored row-major as
<code>[0.5,0.5,-0.5,-0.5]</code>. The backward pass produces a nonzero gradient, yet
equal updates keep the two columns equal.</p>

<p>The condition is equal treatment, not simply the presence of a zero.
Different downstream treatment would remove this particular equality argument.
Zero optional biases and unit normalization gains are separate choices; they do
not make unequal sampled feature columns identical.</p>
<h3 id="reject-an-invalid-request-without-changing-later-draws">Reject an invalid request without changing later draws</h3>
<p>Valid names contain nonempty dot-separated segments of lowercase ASCII letters,
digits, and underscores. The constructor checks the name first, then zero
fan-in, zero fan-out, fan-sum overflow, shape-product overflow, storage
reservation, tensor construction, and trainable-leaf construction. This order
makes the first returned error stable when several inputs are invalid.
The guarantee concerns returned errors; it does not promise recovery from
every possible process allocation abort.</p>

<p><code>NamedParameter::from_tensor</code> offers the same named trainable-leaf boundary
for manually supplied finite values, checking the name before the leaf.
<code>NamedParameters::try_new</code> scans declaration order and reports the earliest
repeated name together with its first index; it does not sort or silently merge
parameters.</p>
<p>The example constructs the query projection first and then the <code>[4,2]</code> token
table on the continuing generator stream. A clone of the projection shares the
original leaf. The independently replayed equal projection has the same values
but a different runtime leaf.</p>

<p><code>Decoder.weight</code> is rejected because its uppercase byte violates the name
grammar. The valid name <code>decoder.invalid.weight</code> with zero fan-in instead
returns <code>ZeroFanIn</code>. Collecting two projection clones repeats their name;
duplicate rejection is a collection operation and consumes no draws. The
example confirms that the rejected sampler calls leave the continuing
generator state unchanged.</p>

<h2 id="separate-measured-weights-from-expected-linear-variance">Separate measured weights from expected linear variance</h2>
<p>Four weights make replay and unequal columns easy to inspect, but they do not
show a distribution’s spread clearly. The figure uses three <code>[64,64]</code>
matrices with <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>4096</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4096</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">4096</span></span></span></span> weights each. The zero matrix uses no draws. The oversized
matrix doubles every seed-<code>17</code> Xavier weight, so the two uniform matrices
have the same base draws and differ only in scale. Their different histograms
therefore isolate the effect of the doubled bound.</p>
<p>All three populations use common equal-width bins. Each cell reports a count
and its percentage of the complete matrix. The measured mean and population
variance come from those finite weights: the calculation finds the mean first,
then divides the sum of squared deviations by the weight count. A sampled mean
need not be exactly zero, and the measured variance need not equal the target.</p>
<p>The depth table uses a different kind of evidence. It starts with independent
zero-centered input features of common unit variance before any layer and follows
expected signal variance through four independent linear layers using the target
weight variances. Each layer assumes independent zero-centered weights with a
common variance, independent of its inputs. Doubling the Xavier bound gives four
times the weight variance, so each such layer multiplies expected signal
variance by four. Zero collapses the signal variance; equal-width Xavier keeps
the expected variance at one. These entries are not measurements from a forward
pass through the sampled matrices or guarantees for the nonlinear residual
decoder.</p>

The paired uniform matrices reuse the same draws; doubling the Xavier bound widens their measured spread. The separate depth table gives expected signal variances from target weight variances, not measured propagation of these samples. It starts with independent zero-centered input features of common unit variance; each independent linear layer uses independent zero-centered weights of common variance, independent of its inputs. In that model, zero weights collapse expected variance, twice-Xavier-bound weights multiply it by four per layer, and Xavier weights keep it unchanged. Repeating the same request reproduces the weights; the selected seed-18 matrix differs from the seed-17 matrix with the matrix request unchanged.</p> </figcaption> <dl class="summary-grid" <p>The important misconception is equating a chosen starting distribution with one
matrix’s exact measured variance, or with a promise that activations can never
vanish or grow. The sampler provides an explicit reproducible baseline; those
stronger claims need separate evidence.</p>

<h2 id="give-the-initialized-matrix-token-lookup-meaning">Give the initialized matrix token-lookup meaning</h2>
<p>Initialization now supplies named trainable matrices with reproducible values
and a declared starting scale. Chapter 18 turns a vocabulary-by-feature matrix
into an embedding table: token IDs select rows, repeated occurrences of an ID
reuse its row, and their gradients scatter-add. Passing vocabulary size and
feature width to this sampler is our table-construction convention, not a
variance derivation for row lookup.</p>
<p>One table is reused across batch items and sequence positions. That shared
parameter identity is separate from the row selected by an individual token ID:
different IDs select different rows, while repeated IDs share a row.</p>
<p>Keep construction order deliberate when several parameters share the
initialization stream. Chapter 21 gives data shuffling a separately owned stream,
Chapter 22 introduces optimizer state, and Chapter 35 persists parameter values
and training provenance. The capability added here is reproducible construction
of trainable leaves; token lookup and parameter updates are later operations.</p> </div> <nav class="chapter-navigation" aria-label="Chapter navigation" data-chapter-navigation <h2 id="from-one-neural-next-word-backward-pass-to-reusable-decoder-vjps">From one neural next-word backward pass to reusable decoder VJPs</h2>
<p>Bengio et al. train a neural next-word model with a learned word-feature table, matrix transforms, a tanh hidden layer, output probabilities, and explicit model-specific backward/update equations. That presentation makes the full learning path inspectable, but Chapter 15’s structural tensor tape still cannot express the lookup, matrix, activation, normalization, and token-loss derivatives needed to train even this small language-model path.</p>
<p>This earlier learned-row path is described by
<a href="https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf">Bengio et al., <em>A Neural Probabilistic Language Model</em></a>.
Bengio et al. build a neural next-word model from learned word-feature rows, matrix equations, a tanh hidden layer, normalized output probabilities, and an explicit backward/update phase for the model parameters.</p>
<p>The fixed calculation above mirrors that inspectable, model-specific style. It
is a new Rust example, not code copied from or attributed to the paper. Adding
a different operation would require editing its whole backward path.</p>
<p>Abadi et al. describe tensor operation graphs whose differentiation finds every path from a loss to parameters and sums partial-gradient contributions, including gathered embedding rows. Vaswani et al. place learned embeddings and the output projection at model boundaries while matrix projections, softmax attention, and nonlinear feed-forward sublayers repeat through the Transformer stack. Shazeer later evaluates Swish with beta one—the same function as SiLU—and SwiGLU variants inside Transformer feed-forward sublayers.</p>
<p>The transition to reusable operation graphs is described by
<a href="https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/osdi16/osdi16-abadi.pdf">Abadi et al., <em>TensorFlow: A System for Large-Scale Machine Learning</em></a>.
Abadi et al. represent operations as graph vertices and tensors as edge values, describe automatic differentiation that sums every backward path to a parameter, and show Gather-based embedding graphs whose gradients update gathered rows.</p>
<p>The Transformer arrangement is described by
<a href="https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2017/file/3f5ee243547dee91fbd053c1c4a845aa-Paper.pdf">Vaswani et al., <em>Attention Is All You Need</em></a>.
Vaswani et al. construct the Transformer from learned embeddings, learned query/key/value projections, attention softmax, two-transform ReLU feed-forward sublayers, and a learned output transform followed by softmax.</p>
<p>The later gated feed-forward step is described by
<a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.05202">Shazeer, <em>GLU Variants Improve Transformer</em></a>.
Shazeer defines Swish as its input multiplied by the sigmoid of beta times that
input, so beta one gives the function also called SiLU; the paper uses it in
SwiGLU Transformer feed-forward variants and reports improved held-out
log-perplexity for gated variants over the studied baseline. The original
Transformer citation uses ReLU; it is not evidence that Vaswani et al. used
SiLU.</p>
<p>This chapter supplies reusable local VJPs for batched matrix products, repeated
row gathers, exp, log, SiLU, stable log-softmax, and combined indexed mean NLL.
Log-softmax and combined indexed mean NLL each retain the probability values
emitted by their own forward call for their VJP instead of normalizing the
logits again.
These operations form the local reverse rules later embedding, projection,
SwiGLU, attention, and token-loss components need; ordinary inference uses only
the forward paths.</p>

<h2 id="save-the-forward-data-each-local-vjp-needs">Save the forward data each local VJP needs</h2>
<p>The public methods extend the Chapter 15 tape instead of constructing a second
graph. <code>TensorValue::gather_rows</code> is the checked public entry for row selection.
The tape first establishes that its table operand is available. For an available
operand, the method validates these facts in order:</p>
<ol>
<li>the table has rank two;</li>
<li><code>index_shape</code> is a valid row-major logical shape and therefore has a known
number of positions;</li>
<li>that position count equals <code>indices.len()</code>; and</li>
<li>each selector, visited in flat order, is smaller than the table’s row count.</li>
</ol>
<p>The flat-order scan reports the first invalid selector. Only after all four facts
hold does the operation append the table width to <code>index_shape</code> and validate the
output shape. In the worked example, table shape <code>[3,2]</code>, <code>index_shape=[4]</code>, and
selectors <code>[1,1,1,2]</code> produce output shape <code>[4,2]</code>.</p>
<p>One crate-private <code>RowGatherPlan</code> then owns the selectors, logical shape, parent
shape, derived output shape, and output element count. Private fields prevent a
public caller from constructing a plan that bypasses those checks. The plan
establishes dimensions and bounds; allocating the output buffer can still fail
separately.</p>

<p>The forward row-copy kernel receives the plan rather than raw selectors and
shapes, so it does not rescan rank, count, or bounds. It materializes independent
row values; the result does not alias the table. After copying succeeds, the
plan’s selectors and shapes move into the saved gather context. “Trusted” here
means that the kernel consumes a value whose private construction established
the facts. It does not mean that public input may be unchecked.</p>

<p>Gather reversal allocates one zero tensor with the parent table’s shape. For
each flat occurrence, it adds the upstream feature row to the destination named
by the saved selector. This is where repeated IDs meet: the forward output rows
are separate values, but their reverse contributions can share a destination.</p>

<p>The other rules follow the same local pattern. Matrix VJPs transpose the final
matrix axes and sum expanded batch contributions back to each parent shape.
<code>exp</code> multiplies by its saved output; <code>log</code> divides by its saved positive input;
SiLU uses its saved input and stable sigmoid.</p>
<p><code>TensorValue::log_softmax</code> makes one checked forward call for two outputs: the
log-probability tensor returned to the caller and the ordinary probability
tensor needed by its VJP. After input validation, one invocation of the checked
group driver computes one statistics bundle per group and emits both tensors
from those shared statistics. The operation saves the emitted probabilities;
backward does not call <code>softmax</code> or normalize the logits again.</p>

<p><code>TensorValue::indexed_mean_nll</code> independently makes one checked forward call for
the scalar mean loss and the probabilities needed by its VJP. After the tape
establishes operand availability, the operation validates the axis, class
extent, target count, nonempty target set, and every target. The
probability module checks every logit for finiteness before allocating the optional probability
tensor so the established error order is preserved. “One forward call” does
not mean one read of each logit: the validation scan computes no maximum,
exponential, sum, or output. The checked group driver then calculates one
<code>RowStats</code> bundle per group with one class scan for the maximum and a separate
class scan for the shifted-exponential sum. The group callback uses that bundle
to accumulate the scalar loss, while the emitter scans the classes to write the
probability tensor retained for the VJP. The saved tensor contains the same
emitted <code>f64</code> values, bit for bit. This is identity of the stored floating-point
values, not a claim of exact real-number arithmetic. Those scans are the steps
of one normalization calculation, not a second normalization call.</p>

<p>At the target class, the parenthesized term subtracts one from the saved
probability. Every class component is then multiplied by the same upstream and
mean scale <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>ˉ</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">/</mi><mi>G</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar L/G</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1.0701em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mord accent"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8201em"><span style="top:-3em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:3em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">L</span></span><span style="top:-3.2523em"><span class="pstrut" style="height:3em"></span><span class="accent-body" style="left:-0.2222em"><span class="mord">ˉ</span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mord">/</span><span class="mord mathnormal">G</span></span></span></span>.</p>
<p>The complete example builds gather, matmul, SiLU, displayed log-softmax, and
combined loss from the values above, then compares its forward and reverse
tensors with the fixed-array calculation. It calls <code>backward_with_trace</code>
because that comparison reads the adjoints of the SiLU output, matrix-product
output, and gathered-row output. Ordinary training uses a lean method:
<code>backward</code> when implicit graph retention is appropriate, or
<code>backward_with_seed</code> when the caller must choose retention or release. The lean
and traced methods use the same reverse calculation; tracing records its results
rather than implementing the local VJPs a second time.</p>

<h2 id="follow-four-occurrence-gradients-into-three-parameter-rows">Follow four occurrence gradients into three parameter rows</h2>
<p>The figure separates the compact forward chain from reverse accumulation. The
fork after SiLU is explicit: log-softmax and combined mean NLL are separate
calls over the same activated logits, and each retains the probabilities from
its own checked forward call. Target rows expose the negative and positive
derivatives, their zero class sum, and the exact parent-gradient shapes through
SiLU and both matrix operands.</p>
<p>The destination-row boxes contain their own occurrence contributions. Row <code>1</code>
contains positions <code>0</code>, <code>1</code>, and <code>2</code> before their sum; row <code>2</code> contains position
<code>3</code>; row <code>0</code> is visibly unused. That arrangement makes it possible to see why
four materialized output rows produce only three parent-table gradient rows.</p>

<h2 id="initialize-the-values-these-gradients-will-train">Initialize the values these gradients will train</h2>
<p>The cumulative implementation can now differentiate a compact chain from
selected embedding rows through a projection, nonlinearity, and stable mean
token loss. This is an operation-level example, not the final decoder architecture:
later feed-forward blocks use SiLU internally, and a separate vocabulary
projection produces the decoder’s loss logits.</p>
<p>Later chapters will package these operations into embedding, linear,
normalization, SwiGLU, and attention layers. Correct gradients still do not
choose useful parameter values. The next problem is choosing initial values
that break symmetry without making signals vanish or explode, so Chapter 17
adds deterministic, scale-aware initialization without adding another VJP.</p> </div> <nav class="chapter-navigation" aria-label="Chapter navigation" data-chapter-navigation data-astro-cid-44eis63d> <p>Before running anything, read the IDs <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>2</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[[2,1,2]]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[[</span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mclose">]]</span></span></span></span> from left to right. The first
and third positions both select row <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span>; the middle position selects row <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span>.
The predicted output is therefore <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>30</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>31</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>20</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>21</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo separator="true">,</mo><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>30</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>31</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[[[30,31],[20,21],[30,31]]]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[[[</span><span class="mord">30</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">31</span><span class="mclose">]</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">20</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">21</span><span class="mclose">]</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">30</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">31</span><span class="mclose">]]]</span></span></span></span>, with shape
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,3,2]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">3</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">2</span><span class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span>. Repetition copies a value into two positions, but it does not create
a second trainable row.</p>
<p>The same matrix <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0576em">E</span></span></span></span> serves all three positions. ID <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span> and ID <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span> select
different parameter rows within that matrix, while the two occurrences of ID
<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span> both select row <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span>. Sharing the table across positions does not make the
rows for different token identities the same parameter coordinates or values.</p>
<p>One-hot notation makes the selection visible. For example, ID <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span> corresponds
to <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,0,1,0]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">0</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">0</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">1</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">0</span><span class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span>. Multiplying that indicator by <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0576em">E</span></span></span></span> leaves <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>30</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>31</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[30,31]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord">30</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord">31</span><span class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span>. The runnable
contrast materializes those zeros only for this tiny explanation:</p>

<p>The numeric distance between IDs is not a semantic distance. IDs <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">1</span></span></span></span> and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span>
are adjacent only in the tokenizer’s numbering; training determines whether
their learned vectors become similar.</p>

<h2 id="from-sparse-identity-to-the-vector-entrance-of-a-transformer">From sparse identity to the vector entrance of a Transformer</h2>
<p>A sparse one-hot word representation assigns one coordinate to each vocabulary item but expresses no graded similarity between words; explicitly carrying that vocabulary-wide vector also wastes work when only one row is needed.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf">Bengio et al., <em>A Neural Probabilistic Language Model</em></a>: Bengio et al. represent the mapping from a vocabulary word index to distributed features as a trainable matrix with one row per vocabulary item and one column per learned feature, share it across context positions, and learn it jointly with next-word prediction.</p>
<p>Bengio et al. learn one dense word-feature matrix jointly with a neural next-word model and reuse that matrix across context positions; each word index still selects its corresponding row. The Transformer retains learned token embeddings for subword tokens, then adds positional information before its stacked attention and feed-forward computations.</p>
<p><a href="https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2017/file/3f5ee243547dee91fbd053c1c4a845aa-Paper.pdf">Vaswani et al., <em>Attention Is All You Need</em></a>: Vaswani et al. use learned embeddings whose width matches the model width for BPE or word-piece tokens and add positional encodings before the Transformer stack; their embedding forward scaling is separate from parameter initialization.</p>
<p>One trainable vocabulary-by-feature matrix is reused at every batch item and sequence position. Each token ID selects its own vocabulary row: different IDs select different rows, while repeated occurrences of the same ID select the same row and accumulate gradients there. Reusing this input matrix across positions is separate from output-weight tying, which remains a later concern alongside positional information, embedding forward scaling, and attention.</p>
<p>One-hot vectors make token identity explicit but carry a vocabulary-sized field
of zeros. Learned dense word features let neural language models share
statistical strength, and Transformers keep learned token embeddings as the
numeric entrance to deeper sequence computation. One embedding matrix is reused
across positions without merging its token rows: different IDs select different
rows, while repeated occurrences of one ID reuse its row and add their gradients
there.</p>
<p>The essential progression is from sparse identity codes to learned vectors.
Parameter sharing here means that every lookup site uses the same matrix, not
that distinct token IDs alias one row. Even if two rows temporarily contain
equal numbers, their token IDs still address different rows and parameter
coordinates. Repeated occurrences of one token reuse its row. A concrete implementation may choose
different integer types, storage layouts, initializers, and error conventions
without changing the lookup or reverse-mode equations. The one-hot product is
an explanatory identity, not a claim that either paper stores those sparse
vectors.</p>

<p><code>Embedding::forward</code> is the public boundary for token IDs supplied as <code>u32</code>.
Because construction has already established the table shape <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>V</mi><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[V,d]</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em"></span><span class="mopen">[</span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.2222em">V</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">d</span><span class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span>, the
method performs these checks in a fixed order:</p>
<ol>
<li>compute the number of positions described by <code>token_shape</code>, rejecting an
invalid or overflowing shape;</li>
<li>require <code>token_ids.len()</code> to equal that position count; and</li>
<li>scan the IDs in flat order, rejecting the first <code>u32</code> value that cannot name
one of the table’s <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6833em"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.2222em">V</span></span></span></span> rows.</li>
</ol>
<p>Only after all IDs pass does the method reserve an owned <code>Vec<usize></code> and convert
the selectors. After the tape establishes that the table operand is available,
the method creates Chapter 16’s crate-private <code>RowGatherPlan</code>. The plan owns the
converted selectors and their logical shape and derives the output shape. Its
trusted constructor does not rescan table rank, selector count, or selector
bounds. The constructor-or-clone invariant supplies the table rank, while this
<code>forward</code> call has just established the selector shape, count, and bounds:</p>

<p>This trust is narrow. The public <code>TensorValue::gather_rows</code> method still checks
table rank, selector shape, selector count, and the first out-of-range selector
for callers that supply raw inputs. A valid plan also does not promise that
memory is already available: allocating the output buffer can still fail. Once
allocation succeeds, the shared kernel performs the row copies and saves the
same plan facts for reverse scatter-add. The embedding layer therefore avoids a
second selector-validation scan without duplicating either the lookup or the VJP.
Only ownership and reuse of checked facts change; output values and shapes,
failure precedence, the lookup equation, saved VJP facts, and repeated-row
gradient addition stay the same.</p>

width without producing values. Shape and count errors are reported before the
first invalid selector. An all-coordinate finite-difference probe with step

<h2 id="follow-every-selection-back-to-its-shared-row">Follow every selection back to its shared row</h2>
<p>The forward half aligns each position with its token ID, one-hot identity,
selected table row, and output vector. The reverse half aligns each upstream
vector with the row that receives it. Row <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="base"><span class="strut" style="height:0.6444em"></span><span class="mord">2</span></span></span></span> appears at two positions, so the
diagram makes the difference visible: its value is copied to two outputs in the
forward pass, while both gradient contributions add into one parameter row in
the reverse pass.</p>

<p>The cumulative model can now turn token-ID tensors into differentiable feature tensors that append one embedding-width axis while keeping one shared named vocabulary-by-feature parameter. 32 later adds that separate relationship by also using the embedding matrix for
the vocabulary projection.

# Mathematical evidence and limits

This is a derivation, not a device or trained-model observation.

For a dense linear output, y_j = sum_i x_i W_ij. With independent, zero-centered
weights, independent zero-centered input terms of common variance, and weight/input
independence, cross terms vanish. Thus Var(y_j) = fan_in Var(W_ij) Var(x_i).
Under analogous backward independence and zero-centered arriving-gradient
assumptions with common gradient variance, the fan_out factor
controls propagated gradient variance. Unit forward and backward multipliers
ask respectively for fan_in Var(W_ij)=1 and fan_out Var(W_ij)=1. These constraints
coincide at equal widths; 2/(fan_in+fan_out) is the stated compromise otherwise.
Near-linear, symmetric activation behavior motivates applying this model; it
does not exactly describe a SiLU/residual/RMSNorm decoder or trained dependent
weights.

A zero-centered real uniform distribution on [-a,a] has second moment a^2/3.
Equating that moment to the target gives a=sqrt(6/(fan_in+fan_out)). Endpoint
closure does not affect the ideal continuous distribution; the actual course
sampler maps a finite binary64 draw grid to a represented interval [-a,a).
A finite matrix need not have exactly the distribution's target variance.
Fans 2+2 give variance 1/2, SD 1/sqrt(2), bound sqrt(3/2). Fans 4+2 give variance
1/3, SD 1/sqrt(3), bound 1. Doubling a uniform bound multiplies distribution
variance by four; four independent equal-width linear layers compound that
multiplier per layer, not as a measured decoder claim.

The tiny zero-symmetry fixture has x=[1,-1], zero weights, SiLU derivative 1/2
at zero, and equal outgoing weights. Both input-weight gradient columns are
[0.5,-0.5]^T. Equal parameter treatment preserves their equality; nonzero
gradients do not alone break symmetry. This is one stated path, not a theorem
that every zero-initialized parameter is unusable.

isolated.value: The forward/backward scale argument assumes independent zero-centered weights, independent zero-centered input features, and zero-centered arriving gradients, each group with its own common variance. The target belongs to the sampling distribution; finite samples need not match it exactly.
